question_details.description:
This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2025-04-10 18:30:00 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/36488). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

On August 16, 2022, President Joe Biden signed into law the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), which [expanded](https://www.epa.gov/green-power-markets/summary-inflation-reduction-act-provisions-related-renewable-energy) the investment tax credits (ITC) for solar-generated electricity to cover all renewable sources, restored its levels to 30% of the project costs, and extended them through 2032. The IRA also established a [domestic content bonus credit](https://www.akingump.com/en/insights/alerts/irs-updates-ptc-and-itc-domestic-content-bonus-guidance) of up to 10% for projects whose steel/iron and a specific percentage of their components were made in the US.

In the wake of the 2024 US elections, Republicans took control of both Houses of Congress and the White House, with President Donald Trump [having expressed interest](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/what-will-happen-to-the-inflation-reduction-act-under-a-republican-trifecta/#the-ira-under-the-incoming-republican-white-house-and-congress) in reducing IRA spending. At the time of this question, congressional Republicans were working on a budget reconciliation bill to possibly enact tax and spending changes to the federal budget (see the Tax Foundation's updated [Budget Reconciliation tracker](https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/federal/trump-tax-cuts-2025-budget-reconciliation/)).

It is important to note that in the House of Representatives, the Republicans hold a slim majority of 220 to 213. In March 2025, a group of 21 Republican representatives [sent a letter](https://www.eenews.net/articles/republicans-mull-thoughtful-phaseout-of-green-credits/) to House Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith to urge him to phase out rather than eliminate the clean energy incentives of the IRA. House Speaker Mike Johnson [told reporters](https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/5167829-johnson-inflation-reduction-act-ira-climate-tax-infrastructure/), in regard to repealing clean energy tax credits among other policies, "It’ll be somewhere between a scalpel and a sledgehammer." It's important to note, too, that reconciliation bills do not always succeed. In July 2017, for example, Senator John McCain famously [cast](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/07/27/us/politics/senate-health-care-vote.html) a decisive No vote to a reconciliation bill that would have repealed parts of the Affordable Care Act.

The Act introduces a new Section 45Y clean‑electricity production credit (CEPTC) and a Section 48D clean‑electricity investment credit (CEITC) that apply to any renewable or energy‑storage facility that begins construction after 2025, with rates tied to a 0 % greenhouse‑gas‑emissions standard.  Energy‑storage facilities gain an election out of the public‑utility property limitation and are treated as five‑year property under MACRS.  The Act also expands the ITC/PTC to energy‑storage, biogas, microgrid controller equipment, and provides a separate PTC for electricity used to produce clean hydrogen under Section 45V.  Wage‑and‑apprenticeship standards can trigger an 80 % credit haircut, while meeting domestic‑content or energy‑community standards can add a 10 % (or 20 % for low‑income communities) credit enhancement.  The Section 45Q carbon‑capture credit is extended to facilities beginning construction before 2033, with a higher rate for direct‑air‑capture.  Fuel‑production credits are extended through 2024 and a new Section 45Z clean‑fuel credit is introduced for 2025‑2027.  The dormant Section 48C investment credit is revived for advanced‑energy production and manufacturing, with a $10 billion ceiling.  The Act creates refundable credits for tax‑exempt entities, allows sale of refundable credits, and changes carry‑over rules to a 3‑year carryback and 22‑year carryforward.  These provisions aim to streamline compliance, incentivize domestic content, and broaden financing options for green projects.

summary: All forecasting experts agree that the probability of domestic content requirements becoming mandatory for obtaining the IRA's Investment Tax Credits (48E) before January 1, 2026, is extremely low—every expert assigns a probability between 1% and 3%. Their consensus is based on multiple overlapping factors: (1) The current Republican-controlled Congress and White House are focused on reducing, phasing out, or eliminating clean energy incentives from the IRA, not making them more restrictive; (2) Recent legislative actions, particularly the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) and related reconciliation efforts, have accelerated phaseouts and narrowed eligibility for tax credits but have not proposed making domestic content requirements mandatory; (3) Industry, bipartisan, and even some Republican actors have lobbied against abrupt increases in compliance burdens, favoring phaseouts or leniency; (4) Treasury and IRS administrative guidance has focused on clarifying or tightening compliance related to phaseouts, not on imposing new mandatory domestic content rules; (5) Historical precedent (base rate) suggests such sweeping new mandates are rare, especially in a political context antagonistic to the underlying policy; and (6) With only 2.5 months left and Congress occupied with other major issues, the legislative and practical barriers are 'very high' or 'near zero' for this sort of change. All experts consider a 'Yes' scenario theoretically possible only via an unlikely last-minute bipartisan compromise, which lacks any supporting evidence or legislative momentum in current news or legislative tracking. In sum, all available indicators point sharply toward a 'No' outcome, and the probability of a mandatory domestic content requirement for the 48E ITC by the deadline is judged to be at the extreme low end of the scale.
